# North African Origins

> How migrations shaped North Africa's population over 20,000 years, told from peer-reviewed ancient-DNA and genome studies, with one Amazigh (Berber) family from Souss-Massa, Morocco, as a worked example.

An independent, non-commercial site. Claims are cited to published literature; where they are not, the page says so. Dates keep their published ranges. Each research summary is an aid to reading, not the paper: cite the paper itself, by its DOI.

## Pages

- [North African Origins | Ancient DNA and migrations](https://northafricanorigins.com/): How 20,000 years of migrations shaped North Africa's population, told from peer-reviewed ancient-DNA and genome studies, with every published date range kept.
- [Start here | North African Origins](https://northafricanorigins.com/start-here.html): Three ways into how migrations shaped North Africa's population: new to DNA, straight to the papers, or the place itself. Pick the one that fits why you came.
- [One family, two lines | E-PF2546 and H1-T16189C!](https://northafricanorigins.com/lineage.html): One Amazigh family, two ancestries: E-PF2546 rooted in Africa for 65,000 years, and H1-T16189C! which crossed from Iberia 8,000-11,000 years ago.
- [What DNA can actually tell you | Haplogroups explained](https://northafricanorigins.com/genetics.html): A haplogroup is not an ancestry percentage. What Y-DNA and mtDNA really trace, where the dates come from, and why published ranges disagree.
- [Culture and language | Tachelhit and the Souss](https://northafricanorigins.com/culture.html): Tachelhit, Tifinagh script, the assembly system and a thousand years of who ruled the Souss — and why the language survived all of it.
- [Maps and sites | Takarkori, Morocco, Souss-Massa](https://northafricanorigins.com/maps-sites.html): Every place named in the research summaries, with satellite and OpenStreetMap links: Takarkori, Moroccan Neolithic sites and the Souss-Massa region.
- [Glossary | Haplogroups, TMRCA, admixture](https://northafricanorigins.com/glossary.html): Plain-language definitions of the genetics terms used across this site: haplogroup, Y-DNA, mtDNA, TMRCA, coalescence, admixture and more.
- [What this evidence cannot show | Limitations](https://northafricanorigins.com/limitations.html): Two haplogroups are two ancestral lines out of more than a thousand. What Y-DNA and mtDNA cannot tell you, and why the dates carry wide error bars.
- [Research and sources | Thirteen papers](https://northafricanorigins.com/research.html): Plain-language summaries of the thirteen peer-reviewed studies behind every population-level claim on this site, each with its DOI.

## Research summaries

13 papers, newest first.

- [A shared selection signal links Canary Islanders and North Africa](https://northafricanorigins.com/research/canary-islanders-exome-ancestry-2026.html): Díaz-de Usera et al., iScience, August 2026, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2026.117146. A whole-exome catalogue of Canary Islanders reports 387,555 genetic variants and a candidate selective sweep around the PRUNE1 gene that the population shares with the North African population it was compared against.
- [North African ancestry in Sicily before the Islamic conquest](https://northafricanorigins.com/research/medieval-sicily-north-african-ancestry-2026.html): Monnereau et al., PLOS One, 24 June 2026, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0350298. Ancient DNA from 111 medieval Sicilians shows that several people buried before the Islamic conquest already carried substantial North African ancestry, so people were crossing the Mediterranean before that conquest.
- [Islamic-period Ibiza reveals North African gene flow](https://northafricanorigins.com/research/mediterranean-islamic-dna-ibiza-2026.html): Rodríguez-Varela et al., Nature Communications, 26 March 2026, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-70615-9. Genomes from medieval Ibiza burials (950–1150 CE) show North African ancestry arriving during the Umayyad and Almoravid periods — movement across the western Mediterranean running north, not south.
- [North African maternal diversity, from 869 mitogenomes](https://northafricanorigins.com/research/north-africa-maternal-diversity-2026.html): Boumajdi et al., Mammalian Genome, 12 March 2026, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00335-026-10209-4. A cohesive Maghreb maternal core, overlaid by historical female-mediated migrations. Directly relevant to how a lineage like H1 sits in the region.
- [733 modern and 43 ancient mitogenomes](https://northafricanorigins.com/research/north-african-mitogenomes-2025.html): Colombo et al., Scientific Reports, 25 July 2025, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-12209-x. A large survey of North African maternal lineages, including the H1 subclade patterns that underlie the maternal half of the family case on this site.
- [The Guanches before European contact](https://northafricanorigins.com/research/canary-islands-amazigh-history-2025.html): Santana et al., Scientific Reports, 3 June 2025, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-04302-y. Demographic history of the indigenous Canarian Amazigh, whose ancestors sailed from North Africa. The same paternal branch as the family case on this site has been reported among them.
- [Punic people were genetically diverse, and barely Levantine](https://northafricanorigins.com/research/punic-genetic-diversity-2025.html): Reich et al., Nature, 23 April 2025, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-08913-3. Genome-wide data from 210 individuals finds Carthaginian-era populations dominated by local and Mediterranean ancestry, with almost no Levantine contribution — culture spread without much migration.
- [Ancient DNA from the Green Sahara](https://northafricanorigins.com/research/green-sahara-ancient-dna-2025.html): Salem et al., Nature, 2 April 2025, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-08793-7. Genomes from Takarkori in Libya, around 7,000 years ago, reveal a deeply divergent North African lineage that had been largely isolated — from a period when the Sahara was grassland.
- [The eastern Maghreb kept its foragers](https://northafricanorigins.com/research/eastern-maghreb-neolithic-continuity-2025.html): Lipson et al., Nature, 12 March 2025, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-08699-4. Ancient DNA from Algeria and Tunisia shows strong continuity of local forager ancestry through the Neolithic transition — farming arrived without replacing the people.
- [Amazigh and Arab populations diverged over 20,000 years ago](https://northafricanorigins.com/research/north-africa-demographic-history-2024.html): Serradell et al., Genome Biology, 30 July 2024, https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-024-03341-4. Whole-genome demographic modelling separates deep Epipaleolithic Amazigh origins from much later Arabization gene flow, via a soft-split model.
- [Amazigh genomic heterogeneity, village by village](https://northafricanorigins.com/research/amazigh-genomic-heterogeneity-2024.html): Vilà-Valls et al., Scientific Reports, 1 May 2024, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-60568-8. The largest Amazigh genomic dataset to date finds diversity at a microgeographical scale, two trans-Saharan admixture waves, and deep Epipaleolithic roots.
- [The Maghreb Neolithic began with migrants from Iberia](https://northafricanorigins.com/research/neolithic-iberia-morocco-2023.html): Villalba-Mouco et al., Nature, 7 June 2023, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06166-6. Ancient DNA from Neolithic Morocco confirms migration across the Strait of Gibraltar — the ancient-DNA reinforcement of the scenario that best explains this maternal line.
- [E-M81 is far younger than anyone expected](https://northafricanorigins.com/research/e-m183-recent-origin-2018.html): Solé-Morata et al., Scientific Reports, 21 November 2017, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-16271-y. Whole Y-chromosome sequencing dates the defining Amazigh paternal marker to roughly 2,000–3,000 years ago, with a star-like pattern indicating rapid expansion from a small founder group.
